1.x: “And when they drew nigh unto Jerusalem..”: Jesus had spent his ministry traveling through Galilee and Judea, often telling people NOT TO broadcast his miracles because his “hour had not yet come.” Now, the timing is deliberate. He arrives at Jerusalem for Passover, the exact time the sacrificial lambs were being chosen. “..come to Bethphage, unto the mount of Olives..”: Bethphage was a small village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. The Mount of Olives carries immense prophetic weight in Hebrew scripture; it is the traditional location from which the Messiah was expected to appear and usher in God’s kingdom (“And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem…”, Zech 14:4 KJV). “..then sent Jesus two disciples”: Jesus is in complete control of the narrative here. He isn’t stumbling into an accidental reception; he is actively orchestrating a specific prophetic event.

2.x: “Go into the village over against you..”: Jesus gives highly specific instructions about the village directly ahead of them (likely Bethphage or nearby Bethany). “...straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her..”: Matthew is unique among the gospel writers because he specifically mentions two animals: a mother donkey (the “ass”) and her young unridden male offspring (the “colt”). It does not contradict the other gospels (Mk 11:2; Lk 19:30; Jn 12:14-15), it simply gives more details about the incident. “..loose them, and bring them unto me”: This display of supernatural knowledge (or pre-arranged planning) shows the disciples that nothing happening in the coming week (even his upcoming arrest) is outside of Jesus’s knowledge or authority. Recall that this foreknowledge comes from the Father, as He chooses to reveal to His human Son (“He that sent me is true; and I speak to the world those things which I have heard of Him”, Jn 8:26 KJV). The Son does not know all things, as he is not omniscient without the divine Spirit of the Father (“But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, neither the Son, but the Father only”, Mt 24:36 KJV).

3.x: “And if any man say ought unto you..”: Mark recorded that this was in fact exactly what happened (Mk 1:5-6). Jesus anticipates that untying someone else’s livestock will naturally look like theft and cause the owners to question the disciples. “..ye shall say, the Lord hath need of them”: The word “Lord” (Kyrios in Greek) here denotes supreme authority. It indicates either that the owners were also believers who would recognize the title, or that the divine authority of the name itself would move their hearts to cooperate. The “Lord” was commonly used for “YHWH,” the God of Israel, since at this point in history the Jews were afraid of uttering the tetragrammaton. The Greek LXX had replaced the Hebrew “YHWH” for the Greek “Kyrios” (Lord). “..and straightway he will send them”: Jesus reassures his disciples that they will face no resistance; the owners will release the animals immediately.

4.x: “All this was done, that it might be fulfilled..”: Matthew wrote his gospel primarily for a Jewish audience. Because of this, he frequently uses “fulfillment formulas” to connect Jesus’s life directly to OT prophecies, proving that Jesus is the long-awaited Messiah. “..which was spoken by the prophets, saying”: Matthew is preparing to quote the ancient scriptures to show that the use of the donkey was a deliberate, prophetic sign.

5.x: “Tell ye the daughter of Sion..”: This is a poetic, prophetic phrase referencing Jerusalem and its inhabitants. Matthew is blending Isaiah 62:11 (“Say ye to the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy salvation cometh”) with Zechariah 9:9 (“Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass,” KJV). “Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek..”: This is the core paradox of the Triumphal Entry. In the ancient world, a conquering king or a military general would enter a city riding a white warhorse, showcasing military might, pride, and judgement. Jesus enters in absolute humility (“meek”). “..and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass”: By riding a donkey, Jesus fulfills Zechariah 9:9 exactly. In ancient Middle Eastern culture, kings rode donkeys when they came on missions of peace, commerce, and goodwill. Jesus is presenting himself as king, but not the political, military revolutionary the crowds were hoping for. He is a KING (v.25), but also a PRINCE of peace (Isa 9:6), coming to conquer sin and death through his own sacrifice. He is both the High Priest AND the Lamb (sacrifice) who enters the most holy place and offers his own blood as the sacrificial lamb: “But Christ came as High Priest….. He appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.. Offered himself without spot to God..” (Heb 9:11-14 KJV).

6.x: This verse highlights the immediate obedience and trust of the disciples. It also demonstrates Jesus’ divine foreknowledge and authority. Everything happened precisely as he said it would.

7.x: The disciples improvised by placing their outer garments (“their clothes”) on the animals to serve as a makeshift saddle for Jesus. Setting a king or leader on a mount with garments underneath was an ancient Near Eastern sign of submission and royal honor (similar to the way Jehu was treated in 2 Kings 9:13).

8.x: The crowd laid their cloaks and freshly cut tree branches (identified as palm branches in Jn 12:13) on the dirt road ahead of Jesus. This was a traditional “red carpet” treatment reserved for conquering heroes and royalty. By laying down their garments and branches (“strawed them in the way” means scattered them on the road), the multitude was publicly declaring Jesus to be their arriving King.

9.x: “Son of David”: The crowd was recognizing Jesus as the rightful heir to King David’s throne, the long-awaited Messiah promised in the OT. “Hosanna”: Derived from a Hebrew phrase meaning “Save, we pray!” or “Save now!”: “Save now(Hoshi’a na), I beseech thee, O LORD: O LORD, I beseech thee, send now prosperity” (Ps 118:25 KJV). Over time, it evolved from a desperate cry for salvation into a joyful shout of praise. But its root meaning is still “Save us!” “Blessed is he…”: The crowd is quoting Psalm 118:25-26, a famous Messianic Psalm. They were acknowledging that Jesus arrived with the absolute authority of God. Notice what the Psalm says: “Blessed be he THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD(YHWH)” (Ps 118:26 KJV). The one who came in the name of YHWH is Jesus (which means YHWH-saves). The Son inherited the name of the Father: “he hath BY INHERITANCE obtained a more excellent name than they” (Heb 1:4 KJV). The Son said: “I will declare THY NAME unto my brethren” (Heb 2:12 KJV), and then declared the name of Jesus. “Wherefore God(YHWH) also hath highly exalted him(the man Jesus), and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of JESUS every knee should bow..” (Phil 2:9-10 KJV). Jesus said: “I am come IN MY FATHER’S NAME” (Jn 5:43 KJV) & “the works that I do in MY FATHER’S NAME, they bear witness of me” (Jn 10:25 KJV). The Son said: “I have manifested THY NAME unto the men” and then manifested the name of Jesus. “Holy Father, protect them by Your name, THE NAME YOU GAVE ME” (Jn 17:11 BSB), “I protected and preserved them by Your name, THE NAME YOU GAVE ME” (Jn 17:12 BSB), so obviously the name of the Father and He gave to His Son is Jesus. “I have made YOUR NAME KNOWN TO THEM and will continue to make it known” (Jn 17:26 KJV), and of course, the only name Jesus gave us is the name of Jesus. So, just like how a NY Police can say: “I come in the name of the NYPD”, likewise the Son comes “in the name of the Father”, aka Jesus, aka YHWH-saves, aka Immanuel (God-with-us). That is why Jesus is the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Jesus is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:10,12), because it is the name ABOVE EVERY NAME (Phil 2:9-10). It is the name of God as He chose to reveal Himself in the New Covenant: “Therefore my people shall know my name(Jesus): therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I” (Isa 52:6 KJV) & “And the LORD shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD, and His name one(Jesus)” (Zech 14:9 KJV). This is why, at the throne, we will see one body: God and the Lamb (the visible Jesus and the invisible divine Spirit of the Father, Rev 22:3) under one face and under one name (Jesus): “And they shall see His face(singular); and His name(Jesus) shall be in their foreheads” (Rev 22:4 KJV).

10.x: “all the city was moved”: THe Greek word used for “moved” is eseisthē (the root word for seismic/earthquake). The entire city violently shaken or stirred up by the commotion. “Who is this?” shows the tension in Jerusalem. While the traveling Galilean pilgrims accompanying Jesus were celebrating, the local Judean establishment and residents were startled, curious, and deeply unsettled by this sudden royal procession.

11.x: “This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth”: The crowds traveling with Jesus answer the city’s question. While they call him a “prophet,” which was a high honor, it also reveals a paradox. They rightly identify his earthly hometown (“Nazareth of Galilee”), but their understanding is still incomplete. They see him as a great prophet and a political deliverer who will overthrow Rome, missing the deeper reality that he is the Son of God (not God-the-Son) who came to save them from sin through his death on the cross just a few days later.

12.x: This commotion was taking place in the Court of the Gentiles, the outer courtyard intended for non-Jewish people to come and pray. “Them that sold and bought”: Jewish Law required travelers coming from far away to sacrifice animals at the temple. Instead of bringing animals on long journeys, travelers were encouraged to buy them in Jerusalem. However, the temple authorities had allowed merchants to set up shop inside the sacred temple walls, effectively turning a place of worship into a noisy livestock market. “The tables of the moneychangers”: Every Jewish man had to pay a yearly temple tax. They could not use common Roman currency (which featured the image of the pagan Emperor) to pay it; they had to exchange it for local Tyrian shekels. The moneychangers charged exorbitant exchange fees, taking financial advantage of religious pilgrims. “Them that sold doves”: Doves were the sacrifices prescribed for the poor who couldn’t afford a lamb or a goat (Lev 5:7). By overthrowing the seats of the dove-sellers, Jesus was specifically pointing out how the merchant system was exploiting the most vulnerable people.

The three Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) all place the cleansing of the temple at the very end of Jesus’ ministry, during his final week before the crucifixion. However, the gospel of John places a temple cleansing at the very beginning of his ministry (Jn 2:13-17). One possible explanation is that Jesus cleansed the temple TWICE: once to inaugurate his public ministry, and a second time to close it out. In this view, Mt 21:12 is the SECOND cleaning. Meaning, if Jesus corrected the temple corruption at the start of his three-year ministry, it is highly likely the greedy practice returned, prompting him to judgmentally bookend his ministry by doing it again. The other explanation is that the cleansing of the temple happened only once, and that either John or the Synoptic gospels moved the story chronologically to make a theological point. Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the cleaning as the “last straw” that directly triggers the religious leaders’ plot to arrest and execute Jesus. John may have placed the event at the beginning of his gospel for thematic reasons, wanting to immediately show his readers that Jesus was superior to the old temple system. Driving out the temple merchants was a massive, disruptive public act. Skeptics of the “two cleanings” theory argue that the temple guard and Roman garrison would have arrested Jesus on the spot if he had tried a stunt like that a second time.

13.x: Jesus doesn’t just act; he defends his actions by weaving together two OT prophecies. “It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer”: This is a direct quote from Isaiah 56:7. God’s design for the temple was to be a sacred, peaceful place where all nations could connect with him. The commercial racket in the outer courtyard completely ruined the environment for prayer. “..but ye have made it a den of thieves”: This draws from Jeremiah 7:11. A “den of thieves” isn’t just a place where robbery happens; it’s a safe haven where criminals hide after they commit crimes. The religious leaders and merchants were using the holy temple as a cover, thinking their religious rituals made their greedy, dishonest lifestyles acceptable to God. By driving out corruption, Jesus was declaring his authority as the Messiah over his Father’s house. He exposed hypocrisy, protected the poor from financial exploitation, and cleared the way so that people could truly seek God without the distraction of greed and commercialism.

14.x: Now that Jesus has driven out the commercial corruption and cleared out the Court of the Gentiles, the space returns to its true purpose: the outcasts enter. Under strict traditional interpretations of the Levitical law and later rabbinic customs, the blind and the lame were often excluded from certain inner parts of the temple area because they were seen as blemished (“The blind and the lame shall not come into the house” 2 Sam 5:8 KJV). Instead of a place that excludes or exploits people. Jesus turns the temple into a place of restoration. He doesn’t just clear out the bad; he fills the empty space with divine mercy and healing. Recall how in Mt 12:45, when a demon left a person, if the person did not fill the void with something good like God, the demon would return with 7 demons that would make his last state worse than the first. With God, there is no neutrality, you either choose what is Good (God), or what is bad (darkness, the absence of Good).

15.x: The religious elite, the chief priests (Sadducees) and scribes (Pharisees), are watching this unfold. They aren’t moved by the blind seeing or the lame walking. Instead, they are deeply offended by the noise. “Sore displeased”: The Greek word aganakteō means to be filled with painful vexation or indignation. They viewed this as blasphemy and a direct threat to their political and religious authority.

16.x: The leaders try to trap Jesus, essentially saying: “Do you hear what they’re calling you? Are you going to let them commit this blasphemy?” Jesus responds with a direct “Yea”, openly accepting the Messianic praise. Then, he exposes their spiritual blindness by quoting Psalm 8:2. “Have ye never read…”: This was a sharp rebuke. These men were the professional Bible scholars of Israel, yet Jesus asks them if they’ve ever bothered to read the Scriptures. Once again, the Scriptures are shown to be the source of truth by Jesus by which everything needs to be examined against. In Psalm 8, the praise of the “babes and sucklings” is directed toward YHWH(God). By applying this scripture to the children praising him, Jesus is not only validating his identity as the Messiah, but he is also subtly pointing to his own divinity. The children saw what the professors missed.

17.x: Jesus does not stay to argue or beg for their approval. He leaves Jerusalem and walks about two miles east over the Mount of Olives to the small village of Bethany. Turning his back on the religious leaders carries symbolic weight. He leaves them to their indignation. Bethany was Jesus’ safe haven during Passion Week. It was the home of his close friends: Mary, Martha, and Lazarus (whom he had recently raised from the dead, Jn 11:1-44). Staying outside the city walls also protected him from a premature, nighttime arrest by the temple authorities before his appointed hour.

18.x: “he hungered”: this verse highlights the absolute authenticity of Jesus’ humanity as “the Son of God” and not as “God-the-Son.” God (the Father, YHWH, Holy Spirit) is an omnipresent Spirit that cannot experience physical hunger, exhaustion, or pain. To redeem humanity, God had to wrap Himself in a genuine human. Therefore, as a man, Jesus experienced every natural limitation of human flesh, yet he was obedient unto death. Jesus, as a man (the flesh, the Son) hungered (v.18), was weary and slept (Mk 4:38), did not know the day or hour of his return (Mk 13:32), he was cold, stripped, and suffered on the cross, and literally died (Mt 27:50). However, Jesus, as God (the divine Spirit/ the Father indwelling), fed 5,000 people (Mt 14:19-21), calmed the storm (Mk 4:39), knew all things (Jn 21:17; Lk 5:22), is the source of all warmth and life sustaining the universe (Col 1:16-17), and raised His own body from the dead (Jn 2:19-21). There are two witnesses in Jesus: the Son (human) & the Father (divine Spirit) - “my judgment is true: for I am not alone, but I and the Father that sent me. It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true. I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me.” (Jn 8:16-18 KJV). These two witnesses are one: “I and my Father are one” (Jn 10:30 KJV), a temple to its Spirit (Jn 2:19-21). Notice the lack of a Trinity.

19.x: “found nothing thereon, but leaves only”: In a healthy fig tree, the young, edible buds appear at the same time as, or slightly before, the leaves. If a tree was covered in lush leaves, a hungry traveler would reasonably expect to find fruit. This tree had the OUTWARD APPEARANCE of fruitfulness, but it was empty. In the OT, the fig tree frequently represents Israel (Hosea 9:10, Jer 8:13). Just the day before, Jesus had cleansed the temple. He found a nation covered in the “leaves” of religious activity (sacrifices, temple rituals, loud chants), but entirely devoid of the "fruit" of true righteousness, justice, and faith. “And presently the fig tree withered away”: The word “presently” here means instantly or immediately. The moment the Creator spoke, the life-fore of the tree began to drain away.

20.x: “How soon..”: The disciples are stunned by the sheer speed of the judgement. A tree usually takes weeks or months to die, dry up, and rot. Jesus’ word bypassed the natural laws of decay, causing the tree to collapse from its roots up within a single day’s span.

21.x: Jesus shifts the focus from the tree to a lesson on spiritual authority and prayer. “..say unto this mountain..”: Jesus was likely pointing directly at the Mount of Olives, where they were standing. In Jewish idioms of the 1st century, a “rooter up of mountains” was a phrase used to describe a great rabbi who could solve impossible difficulties. Jesus transforms this idiom into a literal spiritual truth: with unwavering faith, even seemingly insurmountable barriers (like the corrupt religious system of Jerusalem or the upcoming trials of the cross) can be completely cast aside.

Mark’s account has a chronological challenge. Matthew’s timeline reads as if Jesus curses the tree, it withers immediately on the spot, and the disciples marvel right then and there. Mark’s timeline splits the event over two days: Jesus curses the tree on Monday morning BEFORE cleansing the temple (Mk 11:12-14), they walk past it again on Tuesday morning AFTER the cleansing, and only then do the disciples notice it has withered away (Mk 11:20-21). There are possible explanations for this discrepancy: (1) Matthew’s “Thematic” view: Matthew is famous for organizing his gospel topically rather than strictly chronologically. He frequently compresses events to keep the narrative punchy and focused on a theme. So what actually happened is that on Monday morning, Jesus cursed the tree (as Mark details). It immediately began to die at that exact moment (“presently”). On Tuesday morning, as they walked back, the full extent of the dead, brittle tree became obvious, and Peter exclaimed: “How soon is the fig tree withered away!” Matthew probably chose to tell the story in a compressed way in order to tell the entire story of the fig tree in one seamless narrative block rather than interrupting it with the temple cleansing. He links the cursing and the disciples’ reaction together because his literary focus is on the certainty of Jesus’ word and the lesson on faith. (2) The mechanics of the withering: The Greek word for “presently” (parachrema) means “on the spot” or “immediately.” When Jesus spoke, the curse took effect instantly at the root level. The tree was fundamentally dead the moment he spoke on Monday. However, it wasn’t until the next morning in the full daylight that the disciples saw the total, devastating physical collapse of the foliage. Matthew records the immediate spiritual reality; Mark tracks the day-by-day physical observation. The final harmony of Passion Week shows a perfect sandwich structure: (1) Monday Morning (the Curse): Jesus enters Jerusalem from Bethany, feels hungry, and CURSES the barren, hypocritical fig tree (Mk 11:12-14). The tree immediately begins dying from the roots up. (2) Monday Afternoon (The Temple Cleansing): Jesus enters the temple and casts out the moneychangers (Mt 21:12-13; Mk 11:15-19). This is the historical reality that mirrors the barren fig tree: religious leaves but no fruit. (3) Tuesday Morning (The Lesson on Faith): Returning to the city, the disciples see the tree completely dried up from the roots. They marvel at how fast it happened, prompting Jesus’ teaching on mountain-moving faith (Mt 21:20-21; Mk 11:20-26).

22.x: This concludes the thought from the previous verse about moving mountains. “..believing, ye shall receive..”: Jesus anchors the power of prayer in absolute confidence in God. This isn’t a magical formula to get whatever the human flesh desires. True “believing” prayer is completely aligned with the Spirit of God. When a believer prays under the influence of the Holy Spirit, their requests match God’s Will, making the answer absolute and certain.

23.x: After cleaning the temple and cursing the fig tree, Jesus returns to the temple courts. The religious elites, backed into a corner by his actions, launch a formal counterattack to question his credentials. “..the chief priests and the elders..’: This was a formal delegation from the Sanhedrin, the supreme religious council of Israel. “..by what authority doest thou these things..”: They are demanding to see Jesus’ credentials. By “these things,” they mean: Who gave you permission to ride into town like a king? Who authorized you to disrupt the economy of the temple and kick out the merchants? In Jewish law, teaching without proper rabbinic ordination or acting as a prophet without Sanhedrin approval was a serious offense. They wanted him to say: “God gave me this authority” so they could charge him with blasphemy, or say: “I took it myself” so they could arrest him as a political rebel.

24.x: In 1st-century Jewish debate, answering a trick question with a counter-question was a standard, brilliant legal strategy. Jesus doesn’t dodge their question; he sets up a condition that forces them to reveal their own spiritual bankruptcy before he answers.

25.x: “..from heaven, or of men?” Jesus takes them back to John the Baptist, who had recently been executed by Herod. John’s ministry was the catalyst for the current spiritual awakening in Israel. “Why did ye not then believe him?”: The Sanhedrin’s private huddle exposes their hypocrisy. John the Baptist had explicitly pointed at Jesus and called him the “Lamb of God” (Jn 1:29). If the leaders admitted that John was a true prophet sent by God (from heaven), they would be forced to admit that Jesus’ authority was also from heaven, because John authenticated Jesus.

26.x: “..we fear the people..”: This is an incredibly telling line. The religious rulers did not care about truth; they cared about survival and public relations. The common people loved John and viewed him as a martyred hero. If the elites publicly insulted John’s memory by calling him a fraud, it would likely spark a riot, costing them their comfortable positions under Roman rule.

27.x: “We cannot tell”: This was a humiliating admission for the supreme spiritual court of Israel. Their job was literally to evaluate religious movements, yet they had to plead ignorance to avoid political suicide. “Neither tell I you..”: Jesus exposes them. By refusing to answer, the leaders showed they were not seeking truth, they were playing politics. Jesus is under no obligation to reveal his identity to dishonest judges who refuse to acknowledge what God has already done through John. This passage perfectly contrasts man-made religious authority with divine sovereign authority. The chief priests had titles, robes, political backing, and institutional power, yet they were paralyzed by fear. Jesus had no human credentials, no formal degrees, and no political office, yet he stood in His Father’s temple with absolute, immovable authority.

28.x: Jesus goes on the offensive with the Parable of the two sons. “But what think ye?”: Jesus uses this phrase to hook his listeners’ attention and force them to make a mental judgement. He is setting up a legal trap for the chief priests and elders. “A certain man had two sons…”: In the spiritual interpretation of this parable, the Father represents God(the divine Spirit). The vineyard is a classic OT symbol for Israel and the work of God’s kingdom (“For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel”, Isa 5:7). The two sons represent two distinct groups of people within the nation of Israel.

29.x: “I will not”: This first son represents the open sinners, outcasts, and lawbreakers of society, specifically the publicans (tax collectors) and harlots (prostitutes). Their lives were a blatant, public rejection of God’s law. They initially said “I will not” to God. “..afterward he repented, and went”: When John the Baptist came preaching repentance, these broken outcasts were pricked in their hearts. They changed their minds, turned from their sins, and began to obey God’s call.

30.x: “I go, sir”: This second son represents the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees. They were hyper-religious, dressed in holy garments, and used polite, respectful language (“sir”). They had a massive outward display of saying “yes” to God’s covenant. “..and went not”: Despite their endless religious vocabulary, rules, and lip service, their hearts were completely hard. When God actually showed up in the flesh through Jesus (and previously through John), they refused to step into the vineyard and do the actual work of faith and humility.

31.x: “They say unto him, The first”: The religious leaders easily answer the riddle, not realizing they have just condemned themselves. Then Jesus drops the hammer. He explicitly states that the most despised social outcasts of Judea (the corrupt tax collectors who worked for Rome and the sexually broken) were entering the kingdom of God ahead of the religious elite. God looks entirely at the heart and obedience, not at religious titles or empty verbal professions. The Pharisees were master theologians who knew the letter of the law, but they lacked the spirit of obedience. The first son showed true repentance (a fundamental turning of the mind and direction), which is the very first step in entering God’s kingdom. God prefers a broken sinner who initially fails but ultimately obeys, over a polished religious professional who claims to serve God but refuses to submit to his actual voice.

32.x: This verse is the application of the Parable of the two sons. Having forced the chief priests and elders to admit that the son who actually obeyed was the righteous one, Jesus now names names. “For John came unto you in the way of righteousness..”: Jesus points directly back to John the Baptist. To come “in the way of righteousness” means John lived exactly the kind of holy, disciplined life that the Pharisees and chief priests supposedly valued. He wasn’t a lawbreaker or a radical zealot; he perfectly modeled old-school, prophetic righteousness, fasting in the wilderness and calling people back to God’s Law. “..and ye believed him not..”: Even though John checked all their boxes for what a holy man should look like, the religious elite rejected his message. They were like the second son in the parable: they claimed to love God’s righteousness (“I go, sir”), but when God actually sent a prophet to prepare the way for the Messiah, they refused to lift a finger to obey (“and went not”). “..but the publicans and the harlots believed him..”: The most despised, broken people of Israel (the tax collectors who colluded with Rome and the prostitutes) heard John’s message of repentance. Their lives had been a flat-out “No” to God, like the first son. But when John preached, their hearts broke. They repented, were baptized, and stepped right into the vineyard of God’s kingdom. “..and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not”: This is the most damning part of Jesus’ rebuke. He tells the leaders that they had a front-row seat to an incredible spiritual revival. They saw hardened criminals, corrupt tax men, and broken women completely transform their lives. In a healthy spiritual leader, seeing lives transformed by God should produce joy and self-reflection. But the Sanhedrin was so blinded by pride that even after seeing the undeniable fruit of John’s ministry, they still refused to humble themselves, change their minds, and believe. Jesus draws a sharp line: God does not measure citizenship in His kingdom by your religious resume, your social status, or how long you have been talking about God. He measures it by your willingness to drop your pride, repent of your sins, and believe His Word when it goes forth.

33.x: Jesus teaches the Parable of the Wicked Husbandmen (or tenants). Jesus is speaking to the chief priests and elders in the temple, using a vineyard (a classic OT symbol for the nation of Israel) to illustrate how religious leaders have rejected God’s prophets and, ultimately, will reject His Son. The Householder represents God (the Father, YHWH, the Holy Spirit, the divine Spirit). The Vineyard represents the nation of Israel, specially chosen and cultivated by God. The Hedge, Winepress, and Tower represent God’s intense care and protection. He gave Israel the Law, a system of worship, and a protected land so they could thrive. The Husbandmen are the tenant farmers, representing the religious leaders (priests, scribes, and elders) trusted to care for God’s people. “Went into a Far Country”: God entrusting the leaders with the vineyard and stepping back to let them fulfill their stewardship.

34.x: The Fruits are God’s expected spiritual fruits from Israel: righteousness, justice, and faithfulness. The Servants represent the OT prophets (like Elijah, Jeremiah, and Isaiah) whom God sent over centuries to call Israel and its leaders back to true worship.

35.x: The Treatment of the Servants mirrors the historical reality of how Israel’s leaders treated the prophets. For example, tradition holds that Isaiah was sawn in two, and Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned. The leaders rejected God’s messengers because they didn’t want to give God His due.

36.x: More Servants: This highlights God’s incredible patience. Despite their violence, He didn’t immediately destroy the leaders. He sent more prophets, but the pattern of rejection and abuse continued.

37.x: His Son represents the man Jesus Christ born of Mary. After all the prophets failed to change the leaders’ hearts, God sent the ultimate messenger, His own Son (who is the image and temple of God Himself, who is an invisible Spirit).

38.x: “This is the heir”: The religious leaders recognized Jesus’ authority and power, even if they refused to admit who he truly was. “Seize on his inheritance”: They wanted control over the people and the religious system without having to answer to God or His Messiah. They thought that by killing Jesus, they could keep their power unchallenged.

39.x: “Cast him out.. And slew him”: A direct prophecy of Jesus’ own death. Just a few days after telling this parable, Jesus would be taken outside the city walls of Jerusalem (outside the “vineyard”) and crucified.

40.x: “What will he do unto those husbandmen?”: Jesus sets a brilliant rhetorical trap. He asks the chief priests and elders to pass judgement on the characters in the story, knowing they don’t yet realize the story is about them.

41.x: “He will miserably destroy”: The religious leaders completely agree with the justice of the landowner. They pronounce their own sentence. Historically, this came to pass in 70AD when Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed by the Romans. “Other husbandmen”: This points to the transition of stewardship. Because the Jewish leadership rejected the Messiah, the kingdom would be given to a new leadership: the apostles and the Christian Church (made up of both Jews and Gentiles), who would faithfully produce spiritual fruit for God.

42.x: “Did ye never read”: This was a sharp, ironic sting to the chief priests and scribes, who prided themselves on being the ultimate experts in the Scriptures. The Stone and the Builders: Jesus is quoting Psalm 118:22-23. The “builders” are the religious leaders responsible for constructing the spiritual house of Israel. The “stone” they reject is Jesus himself, whom they view as useless to their plans. “Head of the corner”: The cornerstone (or capstone). It is the single most important stone in a building, tying two walls together and supporting the weight of the entire structure. Jesus is the foundational rock, not Peter. Even Peter says so in his epistle. In 1 Peter 2:4-8, Peter writes: "To whom coming, as unto A LIVING STONE(Jesus), disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious, YE ALSO, AS LIVELY STONES(all believers), are built up a spiritual house… Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion A CHIEF CORNER STONE(Jesus), elect, precious.. Unto you therefore which believe he is precious… And a stone of stumbling, and A ROCK(Jesus is the “petra’) of offence..." Peter identifies Jesus as the living Stone and the Chief cornerstone. Believers are living stones built upon Jesus. Notice that Peter includes himself among the “living stones. He does not single himself out as the unique foundation. Peter is literally quoting Isaiah 28:16: "Behold, I lay in Zion FOR A FOUNDATION A STONE (Jesus, not Peter), a tried stone, a precious corner stone..." He explicitly applies this prophecy to Jesus. Peter agrees with Paul, who says: "...built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being THE CHIEF CORNER STONE." (Eph 2:19-20 KJV). The apostles collectively belong to the foundation, but Christ ALONE is the cornerstone that determines and holds together the building together. Likewise, in 1 Corinthians 3:11: "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." Peter’s sermon in Acts also identifies Jesus (not Peter) as the stone foretold in Scripture: "This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner. Neither is there salvation in any other..." (Acts 4:10-12 KJV). Peter is a “lively stone,” not a foundational Rock. Peter: “Ye ALSO, as lively stones…” (1 Peter 2:5 KJV). The “ye” includes the Christian community to whom Peter writes, and Peter presents himself as one of that same community, not as one holding a special source of authority over them. “Thsi si the Lord’s doing”: Turning a crucified “criminal” into the ruler of the universe is entirely God’s sovereign plan, and it leaves those who see it in awe (marvellous).

43.x: “taken from you..”: This is the direct application of the vineyard parable.
